svg.aria-label: The life of a window buffer. A window has no buffer until it is shown. Showing it allocates a buffer, a kernel area of its own, rounded up to the next 128 pixels in each direction; the window then draws into it. Growing past that size reallocates to the next step and copies what fits. Shrinking to less than half the area reallocates smaller. Hiding or minimizing the window, or leaving the workspace it is on, frees the buffer; the window redraws when it can be seen again. Closing the window frees it too. Each visible window costs width times height times 4 bytes: about 0.5 MB for 400 by 300, 8 MB for 1920 by 1080, and 33 MB for 3840 by 2160. On x86_gcc2h the buffers share app_server's 2 GB address space.
svg.text: The life of a window buffer
Only windows that can be seen have one. Each is a kernel area, so its memory goes back at once.

Measured in VirtualBox: after a stress run app_server used 49.2 MB composited against 46.7 MB stock;
switching to an empty workspace took five buffers (4.6 MB) down to two (3.1 MB). Busy desktops at high
resolutions aren't measured yet. On x86_gcc2h the buffers share app_server's 2 GB address space.
